meta.title: Dust vs. the Signal — TCNJ HuLC
meta.description: TCNJ's NASA Human Lander Challenge capstone project: the project, the team, and past alumni.

home.lede: NASA's Human Lander Challenge is asking teams to solve problems in lunar surface communications equipment — a challenge that leans electrical engineering. The College of New Jersey's team is tackling it from a mechanical angle instead. We're in the research phase now, weighing whether the stronger fix is mitigating the lunar dust and regolith that fouls the hardware, or rethinking its geometry outright.
home.panel_hulc_body: NASA's Human Lander Challenge is a national university design competition run with the National Institute of Aerospace, aimed at the technology NASA needs for its Artemis campaign to return humans to the Moon. Each year NASA opens a new focus area for teams to design against — this cycle (labeled "2027") centers on lunar surface communications equipment. Teams submit proposals, then present forward-phase designs to NASA reviewers.

project.artemis_body: NASA's Artemis campaign is the agency's push to return astronauts to the Moon and build a sustainable presence there ahead of eventual Mars missions. Artemis II carried a crew around the Moon and back in 2026 — the first crewed lunar flight in over fifty years — and NASA is now moving hardware into place for Artemis III, which is planned to put astronauts back on the lunar surface. HuLC exists to pull outside engineering talent, like ours, onto the hardware problems that campaign still needs solved.
project.angle_body_1: This year's HuLC theme (the "2027" cycle) centers on lunar surface communications equipment — an area that leans electrical engineering. Our team is approaching it from a mechanical lens instead, and right now we're still in the research phase: reviewing NASA's technical archives and our own program's past HuLC projects before committing to a direction.
project.angle_body_2: Two candidate directions are on the table: mitigating the lunar regolith and dust that fouls comms hardware over time, or redesigning the equipment's geometry itself — its housing, mounts, or structure — so it holds up on the surface without relying on electronics to do the work.
